text:
The term "heart disease" refers to several types of heart conditions. The
most common type of heart disease in the United States is coronary artery
disease (CAD). CAD affects the blood flow to the heart. Decreased blood
flow can cause a heart attack.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: About Heart Disease

text:
Sometimes heart disease may be "silent" and not diagnosed until a person
experiences signs or symptoms of a heart attack, heart failure, or an
arrhythmia. When these events happen, symptoms may include:

- Heart attack: Chest pain or discomfort, upper back or neck pain,
  heartburn, nausea or vomiting, extreme fatigue, dizziness, and shortness
  of breath.
- Arrhythmia: Fluttering feelings in the chest (palpitations).
- Heart failure: Shortness of breath, fatigue, or swelling of the feet,
  ankles, legs, abdomen, or neck veins.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: About Heart Disease

text:
High blood pressure, high blood cholesterol, and smoking are key risk
factors for heart disease. About half of people in the United States (47%)
have at least one of these three risk factors. Several other medical
conditions and lifestyle choices can also put people at a higher risk for
heart disease, including diabetes, overweight and obesity, unhealthy diet,
physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol use.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: About Heart Disease

text:
Cardiac rehabilitation is an important program for anyone recovering from a
heart attack. This can also include heart failure, or some types of heart
surgery. Cardiac rehabilitation is a supervised program that includes
physical activity, education about healthy eating, taking medicine as
prescribed, ways to help quit smoking, and counseling to find ways to
relieve stress and improve mental health. A team of people may help
through cardiac rehabilitation, including the health care team, exercise
and nutrition specialists, physical therapists, and counselors or mental
health professionals.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: About Heart Disease

text:
1 out of every 5 (22%) deaths in the United States is due to heart disease,
making it the leading cause of death in the United States.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: About Heart Disease

text:
Several health conditions, lifestyle, and age and family history can
increase risk for heart disease. These are called risk factors. Key risk
factors for heart disease include high blood pressure, high cholesterol,
and smoking. Some risk factors cannot be controlled, such as age or family
history, but steps can be taken to lower risk by changing the factors that
can be controlled.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

text:
High blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart disease. It happens
when the pressure of the blood in the arteries and other blood vessels is
too high. If not controlled, it can affect the heart and other major
organs, including the kidneys and brain. High blood pressure is often
called a "silent killer" because it usually has no symptoms — the only way
to know is to measure it. It can be lowered with lifestyle changes or
medicine.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

text:
Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance made by the liver or found in
certain foods. If more cholesterol is taken in than the body can use, the
extra cholesterol can build up in the walls of the arteries, including
those of the heart, leading to narrowing of the arteries and decreased
blood flow to the heart, brain, kidneys, and other parts of the body.

There are two main types of blood cholesterol:
- LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol — considered "bad" cholesterol
  because it can cause plaque buildup in the arteries.
- HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol — considered "good"
  cholesterol because higher levels provide some protection against heart
  disease.

High blood cholesterol usually has no signs or symptoms — the only way to
know is a blood test called a "lipid profile."
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

text:
The body needs glucose (sugar) for energy, and insulin (made in the
pancreas) helps move glucose from food into the body's cells. In diabetes,
the body doesn't make enough insulin, can't use its own insulin as well as
it should, or both — causing sugar to build up in the blood. The risk of
death from heart disease for adults with diabetes is higher than for
adults who do not have diabetes.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

text:
Obesity is excess body fat. It is linked to higher "bad" cholesterol and
triglyceride levels and lower "good" cholesterol levels, and can lead to
high blood pressure and diabetes as well as heart disease.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

text:
Eating a diet high in saturated fats, trans fat, and cholesterol has been
linked to heart disease and related conditions such as atherosclerosis.
Too much salt (sodium) in the diet can raise blood pressure. Not getting
enough physical activity can lead to heart disease and increase the
chances of other risk factors (obesity, high blood pressure, high
cholesterol, diabetes). Drinking too much alcohol can raise blood pressure
and triglyceride levels. Tobacco use increases the risk for heart disease
and heart attack — nicotine raises blood pressure, and carbon monoxide
from cigarette smoke reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

section_title: Genetics, age, sex, race and ethnicity
text:
Genetic factors likely play some role in high blood pressure, heart
disease, and related conditions, though people with a family history of
heart disease also often share common environments and other risk factors.
Risk increases even more when heredity combines with unhealthy lifestyle
choices. Heart disease is the number one killer of both men and women, can
happen at any age, and risk goes up with age. Heart disease is the leading
cause of death for people of most racial and ethnic groups in the United
States, including African Americans, American Indians and Alaska Natives,
and White people; for Asian American, Pacific Islander, and Hispanic
people, it is second only to cancer.
source: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
title: Heart Disease Risk Factors

section_title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects
text:
*Note: unlike the CDC/NHLBI documents elsewhere in this knowledge base,
MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia articles are A.D.A.M.-licensed content,
not a direct U.S. federal government work — this file is an original
paraphrase, written specifically to close a retrieval gap found during
real testing (the knowledge base had no document explaining what a
"reversible defect" finding actually means, even though it's one of the
ML model's most predictive features).*
source: MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine, NIH) and other NIH-affiliated sources — paraphrased summary
title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects (paraphrased summary)

text:
A nuclear (thallium or similar tracer) stress test evaluates blood flow to
the heart muscle by injecting a small amount of radioactive tracer into
the bloodstream, then imaging how that tracer distributes through the
heart — once at rest, and once during stress (exercise on a treadmill, or
a medication that simulates exercise for patients who can't exercise). A
scanning camera captures both sets of images so they can be compared side
by side.
source: MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine, NIH) and other NIH-affiliated sources — paraphrased summary
title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects (paraphrased summary)

text:
A "reversible defect" is a region of the heart muscle that shows reduced
tracer uptake during the stress images but normal (or substantially
improved) uptake in the rest images. This pattern indicates that part of
the heart muscle is getting enough blood at rest, but not enough when
demand increases during exertion — usually because a coronary artery
supplying that region is narrowed (though not fully blocked) by plaque.
The tissue itself is still alive and viable; it's under-supplied only
under increased demand. Clinically, a reversible defect is treated as a
signal of current, active ischemia — reduced blood flow to living tissue —
which is why it appears as a strong predictor in models like this
project's: it corresponds to a coronary artery that is significantly, but
not completely, obstructed.
source: MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine, NIH) and other NIH-affiliated sources — paraphrased summary
title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects (paraphrased summary)

text:
A "fixed defect" is a region that shows reduced tracer uptake in BOTH the
stress and the rest images — the pattern doesn't change between the two.
This usually indicates permanently scarred heart tissue from a prior heart
attack: dead or scarred muscle doesn't take up the tracer well regardless
of how much blood is reaching it, because the tissue itself, not the blood
supply in the moment, is the limiting factor. (In a minority of cases, a
fixed-looking defect can also be a technical artifact — e.g. from breast
or diaphragm tissue blocking part of the imaging — which is one reason
results are read alongside other information, not in isolation.)
source: MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine, NIH) and other NIH-affiliated sources — paraphrased summary
title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects (paraphrased summary)

text:
Reversible and fixed defects point to different underlying problems and
different treatment implications: a reversible defect suggests a
narrowing that is actively restricting blood flow under demand and may be
a target for further intervention, while a fixed defect more often
reflects prior, established damage. Both are distinct from the vessel
blockage count seen on a coronary angiogram (the `ca` feature elsewhere in
this project's dataset) — angiography shows which vessels are physically
narrowed, while a nuclear stress test shows the functional consequence
(whether the heart muscle those vessels feed is actually under-supplied).
The two tests are complementary, not redundant, which is part of why both
show up as independently predictive features in this project's model.
source: MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine, NIH) and other NIH-affiliated sources — paraphrased summary
title: Nuclear Stress Test — Reversible vs. Fixed Defects (paraphrased summary)

text:
Angina, also known as angina pectoris, is chest pain or discomfort that
occurs when part of the heart muscle does not get enough oxygen-rich
blood. It is a common symptom of coronary heart disease, which develops
when the arteries of the heart become partially or totally blocked.

Angina pain can feel like pressure, squeezing, tightness, or burning in
the chest. The discomfort can also spread to the shoulders, arms, neck,
jaw, or back, just like a heart attack. Angina pain can even feel like an
upset stomach. Symptoms can be different for women and men. Angina is very
common, affecting approximately 11 million people in the United States.
There are several types of angina, and symptoms may vary depending on
which type a person has. Angina pain, also called an angina event, can
happen when the heart is working hard, or it can happen at rest.

Angina can be a warning sign of a higher risk of having a heart attack.
Chest pain that does not go away requires immediate emergency care.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Angina (Chest Pain) - What Is Angina?

text:
To diagnose angina, a healthcare provider will ask about symptoms and may
order blood tests, take an X-ray image, and do tests such as an
electrocardiogram (ECG) or an exercise stress test to find out how well
the heart is working. With some types of angina, emergency medical
treatment may be needed to prevent or treat a heart attack.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Angina (Chest Pain) - What Is Angina?

text:
Angina is not itself a disease, but a symptom of an underlying heart
problem. Coronary artery disease — plaque building up inside the large
arteries that supply blood to the heart (atherosclerosis) — is a common
cause; the plaque narrows or blocks the arteries, reducing blood flow to
the heart muscle. Coronary microvascular disease, in which the tiny
arteries branching off the larger coronary arteries are damaged or unable
to expand as usual when the heart muscle needs more oxygen-rich blood, can
also cause angina.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Angina (Chest Pain) - What Is Angina?

text:
Both women and men having angina or a heart attack often describe their
chest pain as crushing, or feeling like pressure, squeezing, or tightness.
In men, angina tends to worsen with physical activity and go away with
rest. Women are more likely to have angina during routine daily activities
rather than during exercise, and mental stress is more likely to trigger
angina pain in women than in men. Other symptoms more common for women
include nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, sleep
problems, tiredness, and lack of energy. Women are also more likely to
have coronary microvascular disease, which can make angina harder to
identify and cause delays in treatment.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Angina (Chest Pain) - What Is Angina?

text:
To help manage angina, a provider may discuss heart-healthy lifestyle
changes, medicines, medical procedures, and cardiac rehabilitation.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Angina (Chest Pain) - What Is Angina?

text:
A healthcare provider diagnoses high blood cholesterol based on medical and
family history, a physical exam, and a blood test of cholesterol levels.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Blood Cholesterol - Diagnosis

text:
A provider will ask about eating habits, physical activity, family
history, medicines, and other risk factors for heart or blood vessel
disease. During the physical exam, the provider will check for signs of
very high blood cholesterol, such as xanthomas (fatty deposits under the
skin), or signs of other conditions that can cause high cholesterol.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Blood Cholesterol - Diagnosis

text:
A provider may order a blood test called a lipid panel (also called a
lipoprotein panel or lipid profile) to screen for unhealthy cholesterol
levels. Fasting for 8 to 12 hours beforehand may be required. A lipid
panel measures:

- **Total cholesterol**
- **LDL ("bad") cholesterol** — the main source of cholesterol buildup and
  blockages in the arteries
- **HDL ("good") cholesterol** — helps decrease cholesterol blockages in
  the arteries
- **Triglycerides** — another type of fat in the blood

The goal for a healthy lipid profile is generally non-HDL cholesterol
below 130 mg/dL, with HDL of at least 40 mg/dL for men and 50 mg/dL for
women (individual targets vary — check with a provider).

### Recommended screening frequency

- **Age 19 or younger**: screening begins at ages 9–11, repeated every 5
  years (as early as age 2 if there is a family history of high
  cholesterol, heart attack, or stroke).
- **Ages 20–65**: younger adults screened every 5 years; men ages 45–65
  and women ages 55–65 screened every 1–2 years.
- **Older than 65**: screened every year.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Blood Cholesterol - Diagnosis

text:
An Lp(a) test is not usually part of a routine lipid panel. High Lp(a)
levels may indicate higher risk of heart or blood vessel disease even if
other cholesterol levels are healthy. Lp(a) level is largely determined by
inherited genes and is unlikely to change much from childhood to old age.
A provider may order this test if there is a family history of stroke or
early heart disease, or an unknown family medical history. If Lp(a) is
high, a provider may prescribe a statin even if other cholesterol levels
are in the healthy range.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Blood Cholesterol - Diagnosis

text:
A healthcare provider will diagnose coronary heart disease based on
symptoms, medical and family history, risk factors, and the results of
heart tests. Providers will likely screen for coronary heart disease at
regular checkups, and may use an app to assess the chance of developing
heart disease in the next 10 years or beyond.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text:
Screening tests and risk assessments for coronary heart disease should
start around age 20 for people without risk factors. Children with risk
factors such as obesity, low levels of physical activity, or a family
history of heart problems may need screening. To screen for coronary heart
disease, a provider may:

- Assess risk factors to evaluate the chance of developing coronary heart
  disease.
- Calculate body mass index and waist circumference to help determine
  whether a person has overweight or obesity.
- Check blood pressure to see whether it is elevated (high blood pressure,
  also called hypertension).
- Order blood tests to see whether cholesterol, triglycerides, or blood
  sugar levels indicate diabetes risk.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text:
Providers may use a risk calculator to estimate cardiovascular risk score
— the chances of having a heart attack, having a stroke, or dying from
heart disease in the next 10 years or more. Risk assessments should be
repeated every 4 to 6 years in adults who do not have heart disease. A risk
score uses data from many people with similar risk factors: even a high
risk score does not mean something bad will definitely happen — for
example, a 10-year risk score of 15% means that, on average, 15 out of 100
people in that risk category will have a heart problem within 10 years.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text:
If a person has symptoms or a family history of coronary heart disease, a
provider may order blood tests (cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoproteins,
sugar, or proteins that are signs of inflammation) as well as heart tests:
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text:
- **Electrocardiogram (ECG)**: records the strength and timing of
  electrical signals as they pass through the heart, and determines
  whether the heart's rhythm is steady or irregular.
- **Coronary calcium scan**: a type of cardiac CT scan that measures the
  amount of calcium in the walls of the coronary arteries; can help assess
  coronary heart disease risk for people who smoke or who do not have
  symptoms.
- **Stress tests**: check the heart while it is working hard and beating
  quickly, typically by walking/running on a treadmill or pedaling a
  stationary bike (or medicine, if a person cannot exercise). An ECG or
  another imaging test checks for low blood flow to the heart muscle
  during the test.
- **Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)**: detects tissue damage or
  problems with blood flow in the heart or coronary arteries; can help
  diagnose microvascular disease as well as nonobstructive or obstructive
  coronary artery disease.
- **Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) scan**: assesses blood flow
  through the coronary blood vessels and into the heart muscle; can help
  diagnose coronary microvascular disease.
- **Coronary CT angiography**: an imaging test that looks at blood flow
  through the coronary arteries using X-ray.
- **Invasive coronary angiography**: uses contrast dye, injected via
  cardiac catheterization, to detect blockages in the coronary arteries;
  often used if other tests show a person is likely to have coronary
  artery disease.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text: Test results may show how much plaque is clogging the coronary arteries.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Coronary Heart Disease - Diagnosis

text:
An electrocardiogram, also called an ECG or EKG, is a simple, painless
test that detects and records the heart's electrical activity. An EKG can
show how fast the heart is beating, whether the rhythm of the heartbeats
is steady or irregular, and the strength and timing of the electrical
impulses passing through each part of the heart. An EKG may be done as
part of a routine exam to screen for heart disease, and may be recorded in
a doctor's office, outpatient facility, hospital before major surgery, or
as part of stress testing.

For the test, the person lies still on a table while electrodes are
attached to the skin on the chest, arms, and legs; the electrodes connect
by wires to a machine that records the heart's electrical activity on
graph paper or a computer. An EKG has no serious risks — it does not give
off electrical charges or shocks. Used for diagnosing arrhythmias, atrial
fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, congenital heart defects, heart attack, heart
failure, and heart valve diseases.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
Holter and event monitors are small, portable electrocardiogram devices
that record the heart's electrical activity for long periods of time
during normal daily activity. They help diagnose arrhythmias (irregular
heartbeats) and check whether treatments for them are working.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
A stress test measures how healthy the heart is and how well it works
during physical stress. Some heart problems are easier to identify when
the heart is working hard to pump blood, such as during exercise. A
provider may recommend this test for symptoms such as shortness of
breath, chest pain, dizziness, or a rapid or irregular heartbeat. If a
problem is found, the stress test can also help choose the right treatment
plan and determine what types of physical activity are safe.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
The test usually involves walking on a treadmill or riding a stationary
bicycle; if a person cannot exercise, medicine is given to make the heart
work hard and beat faster, simulating exercise. Electrodes are placed on
the chest, a blood pressure cuff on the arm, and a pulse monitor on a
finger or elsewhere; heart activity and blood pressure are measured before
the test begins. The person then gradually increases treadmill speed or
bicycle resistance until the heart reaches a target heart rate for their
age. Most stress tests include an electrocardiogram (to measure electrical
activity and heart rate) and a blood pressure monitor throughout exercise,
which typically lasts about 10 to 15 minutes. The test is stopped early if
there is any sign of a heart problem or if the person is too tired to
continue. Providers may also use echocardiography, cardiac MRI, or a
nuclear heart scan to image the heart during or right after the stress
test, showing how well blood flows through the heart and how well it pumps
when it beats.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
After the test, heart activity and blood pressure are measured again to
confirm they return to normal range. Intense exercise during the test can
rarely cause chest pain or irregular heartbeats, which usually resolve
after exercise stops. Used for diagnosing angina (chest pain), arrhythmias,
coronary heart disease, heart failure, and heart valve diseases.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
Coronary angiography is a procedure that uses contrast dye (usually
iodine-based) and X-ray pictures to detect blockages in the coronary
arteries caused by plaque buildup, which prevent the heart from getting
oxygen and nutrients. It is used to diagnose heart disease or follow up on
abnormal results from an ECG or exercise stress test, and can help plan
treatment during a heart attack. The procedure is done via cardiac
catheterization: a catheter tube is inserted into a blood vessel (arm,
groin/upper thigh, or neck), guided into the coronary arteries using X-ray
imaging, and contrast dye is injected to highlight blockages. If
blockages are found, percutaneous coronary intervention (coronary balloon
angioplasty, often with a stent) may be used to improve blood flow.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
Echocardiography ("echo") is a painless test using sound waves to create
moving pictures of the heart, showing its size, shape, and how well it is
pumping blood. Doppler ultrasound, a type of echo, shows how well blood
flows through the heart's chambers and valves. Stress echocardiography is
done as part of a stress test, comparing heart images before exercise and
immediately after, to see whether parts of the heart muscle work less well
when the heart rate increases — a sign that part of the heart may not be
getting enough blood or oxygen due to narrowed or blocked arteries.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: Heart Tests

text:
Everyone age 3 or older should have blood pressure checked by a healthcare
provider at least once a year. Regular checks can also show how well
treatment for high blood pressure is working. Preparation for an accurate
measurement includes: no exercise, coffee, or cigarettes for 30 minutes
before the test; using the bathroom beforehand; sitting relaxed for at
least 5 minutes with feet flat on the floor; not talking during the test;
and resting the arm at heart level. Readings can be inaccurate due to
"white coat hypertension" (higher readings in a provider's office than at
home), "masked high blood pressure" (lower readings at the office than
elsewhere), or an incorrectly sized cuff.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: High Blood Pressure - Diagnosis

text:
Blood pressure is reported as two numbers: the top (systolic) number,
measured when the heart pumps and pressure is highest, and the bottom
(diastolic) number, measured between heartbeats when pressure is lowest —
for example, "120 over 80." For most adults, a healthy blood pressure is
less than 120/80 mm Hg. Research has shown that systolic blood pressure
higher than 120 mm Hg can cause harm to health over time, including organ
damage. Readings above 180/120 mm Hg are dangerously high and require
immediate medical attention.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: High Blood Pressure - Diagnosis

text:
| Category | Systolic (mm Hg) | | Diastolic (mm Hg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | Less than 120 | AND | Less than 80 |
| Elevated | 120–129 | AND | Less than 80 |
| High Blood Pressure Stage 1 | 130–139 | OR | 80–89 |
| High Blood Pressure Stage 2 | 140 or higher | OR | 90 or higher |
| Hypertensive Crisis | Higher than 180 | OR | Higher than 120 (seek immediate care) |
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: High Blood Pressure - Diagnosis

text:
Two or more blood pressure readings at separate medical appointments are
generally needed to diagnose high blood pressure. A provider may also ask
about eating patterns, physical activity level, sleep, body weight,
stress, smoking status, and family health history to understand risk
factors and set up a treatment plan, and may order further tests to check
whether high blood pressure has already affected other organs.
source: NHLBI (National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute), NIH
title: High Blood Pressure - Diagnosis

text:
*Note: unlike the other documents in this knowledge base, WHO fact sheet
content is not a U.S. federal government work and is not automatically
public domain. This file is written as an original paraphrase of publicly
reported WHO statistics and guidance, not a verbatim copy, and should be
treated as a lower-precision citation source than the CDC/NHLBI documents
in this knowledge base — check the source URL for exact current figures.*
source: World Health Organization (WHO)
title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) — Fact Sheet (paraphrased summary)

text:
Cardiovascular diseases are described by WHO as the leading cause of death
globally. WHO's cardiovascular disease work sits within its broader effort
against noncommunicable diseases, which together account for a large share
of deaths worldwide, and cardiovascular disease alone is estimated to
cause on the order of tens of millions of deaths annually. A large
majority of cardiovascular deaths are attributed to heart attacks and
strokes, and a substantial share occur prematurely, in people under 70.
source: World Health Organization (WHO)
title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) — Fact Sheet (paraphrased summary)

text:
WHO identifies the most important behavioral risk factors for heart
disease and stroke as: unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use,
and harmful use of alcohol. Air pollution is highlighted as a significant
environmental risk factor. These behavioral and environmental exposures
tend to show up in individuals as intermediate risk factors — raised blood
pressure, raised blood glucose, raised blood lipids, and overweight or
obesity — which can be measured in primary care settings and signal
increased risk of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, and other
complications.
source: World Health Organization (WHO)
title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) — Fact Sheet (paraphrased summary)

text:
WHO guidance emphasizes that stopping tobacco use, reducing dietary salt,
eating more fruit and vegetables, engaging in regular physical activity,
and avoiding harmful alcohol use have all been shown to reduce
cardiovascular disease risk. High blood pressure in particular is
highlighted by WHO as one of the largest single contributors to
cardiovascular deaths worldwide.
source: World Health Organization (WHO)
title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) — Fact Sheet (paraphrased summary)

section_title: Why this document is included despite the licensing caveat
text:
The ML model and CDC/NHLBI documents in this knowledge base are U.S.
population-derived and U.S.-context. Including a paraphrased WHO summary
gives the agent a way to add brief global-context framing (e.g., "this
risk factor is also flagged as significant globally by WHO") without
overstating precision — the agent's Risk Explanation Tool should treat
this file as directional context, not a source for exact statistics.
source: World Health Organization (WHO)
title: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) — Fact Sheet (paraphrased summary)
